0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
If Bordeaux is the stage of Cabernet Sauvignon, then Touraine in the Loire Valley is the true spiritual home of Cabernet Franc. The three AOCs Chinon, Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil are laid out in a triangle where the Loire and Vienne rivers meet, each with different soils, making elegant reds of very different character.

Learning Objectives

🪨 Grasp the soil differences of the three AOCs

How gravel (graviers), tuffeau and clay-limestone (argilo-calcaire) shape Cabernet Franc of different personalities

🍷 Understand the aromatic fingerprint of Cabernet Franc

The origins and recognition of typical aromas such as violet, pencil shavings (graphite), red berries and pepper

🏰 Know representative producers

Learn the style and philosophy of legendary Loire estates such as Charles Joguet and Clos Rougeard
1.title: Chinon — Three Soils, Three Faces
1.highlights.0.title: Gravel flats (Graviers)
1.highlights.0.content: Sandy gravel, fast drainage, producing light, easy-drinking wines with fresh strawberry and floral notes; most appealing when young, with moderate ageing potential
1.highlights.1.title: Tuffeau slopes (Coteau)
1.highlights.1.content: South-facing tuffeau slopes with plenty of sunshine, producing the most complex and rich Chinon, which can age 10–20 years
1.highlights.2.title: Plateau clay-limestone (Plateau)
1.highlights.2.content: Heavy clay on the plateau, a cold soil, producing the most structured version, with firm tannins that need time to show
1.content:
The greatness of Chinon AOC is that the same variety (Cabernet Franc) shows very different personalities on three different soils. Understand the soils of Chinon and you understand the essence of Loire terroir.

Gravel flats (alluvial soils of the Loire and Vienne river banks): quick to reach ripeness, making light, fruity wines for early drinking. Typical sites: Les Closeaux, Clos de la Dioterie.

Tuffeau slopes (south-facing slopes): the finest zone of Chinon, with plenty of sunshine, strong minerality and the highest complexity. Typical sites: Clos de l'Écho, Clos du Chêne Vert (Charles Joguet's legendary vineyards).

Plateau clay-limestone (plateau argilo-calcaire): heavy, cold soil; late-ripening grapes and the firmest tannins, needing 5–10 years to show complexity.

The estate Charles Joguet (since 1957) pioneered single-site bottlings (crus), showing the world what Chinon's soil differences make possible. His approach influenced the move to fine wine across the whole Touraine region.
2.title: Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
2.highlights.0.content: On the north bank of the Loire, with mixed tuffeau and gravel soils, showing both red and black fruit; a structure slightly weightier than Chinon, with some wines ageing 15–20 years
2.highlights.1.content: An independent AOC next to Bourgueil (also on the north bank of the Loire), mainly sandy gravel, the lightest soils and the lightest wines, with red fruit and florals; the best suited to young drinking of the three
2.content:
Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil are both on the north bank of the Loire and almost adjacent geographically, yet clearly differ in style because of soil differences.

Bourgueil's tuffeau slopes give wines more minerality and an ageing frame, while its gravel lowlands produce fresh fruity wines. Top estates: Domaine de la Chevalerie (traditional large-cask ageing, high complexity), Domaine Yannick Amirault.

Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil is mainly sandy gravel (sables et graviers), extremely well drained, where temperatures rise relatively faster, so Cabernet Franc ripens earlier, with more fresh red fruit (strawberry, raspberry) and florals (violet) and supple tannins — a perfect red for restaurants to open and drink right away.

Comparing tasting notes

🔴 Bourgueil (tuffeau): black plum, cedar, tobacco, minerality, powerful structure, needing 3–5 years to begin showing

🌸 Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil: strawberry, violet, slight green pepper, airy and light, ready to drink on opening
3.title: The Aromatic Fingerprint of Cabernet Franc
3.content:
Cabernet Franc's aromas in the Loire are completely different from Bordeaux versions — there is no new-oak vanilla, but the purest personality of the variety:

🌸 Primary aromas (variety and fermentation)

  • Violet, rose — Cabernet Franc's signature floral notes
  • Strawberry, raspberry, redcurrant — fresh red berries
  • ✏️ Pencil shavings (graphite) — Chinon's mineral "fingerprint"
  • 🌿 Slight green pepper (pyrazine) — the mark of vintages that were not fully ripe; in small amounts it adds complexity

🔄 Secondary aromas (ageing evolution)

  • Leather, tobacco — mineral evolution after 5–10 years of ageing
  • Dried rose, dried spices — complexity from oxidative ageing
  • Mushroom, forest floor — the earthy aromas of old wines

Learn to recognise the triangle of "pencil shavings + violet + red berries," the most reliable identity code of Chinon and Bourgueil.
4.title: Quiz
4.questions.0.question: Of Chinon's three soils, which produces the most complex wines with the greatest ageing potential?
4.questions.0.options.0: Gravel flats (graviers) — good drainage, fresh fruit
4.questions.0.options.1: Tuffeau slopes (coteau) — south-facing sunshine, the strongest minerality
4.questions.0.options.2: Plateau clay-limestone (plateau) — the heaviest soil, the firmest tannins
4.questions.0.options.3: The three soils are identical in quality
4.questions.0.explanation: The tuffeau slopes (tuffeau coteau), thanks to south-facing sunshine and mineral-rich soils, produce Chinon's most complex wines with the greatest ageing potential, such as Charles Joguet's Clos du Chêne Vert and Clos de l'Écho.
4.questions.1.question: What is the main stylistic difference between Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil and Bourgueil?
4.questions.1.options.0: Different varieties — Saint-Nicolas uses Gamay, Bourgueil uses Cabernet Franc
4.questions.1.options.1: Saint-Nicolas has more sandy-gravel soil and a lighter, more floral style; Bourgueil has more tuffeau and a weightier structure
4.questions.1.options.3: Saint-Nicolas is sweet, Bourgueil is dry
4.questions.1.explanation: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil is mainly sandy gravel (sables et graviers), producing lighter, more floral wines; Bourgueil has more tuffeau slopes, producing weightier, age-worthy wines. Both are led by Cabernet Franc.
